title: Six Senators Urge Trump to Immediately Reverse Russian Diesel Export Plan】
body:
WASHINGTON — A bipartisan coalition of six U.S. senators has formally urged the Trump administration to scrap a proposed deal to import diesel fuel from Russia, arguing that the plan undermines national security and contradicts the broader strategy to curb soaring gasoline prices. The letter, signed by four Republicans and two Democrats, calls for an “immediate reversal” of the policy, which the White House introduced in late June as a stop‑gap measure to ease domestic fuel shortages and temper inflationary pressures on American consumers.

The proposal, initially floated by the Energy Department, would see the United States purchase up to 1 million barrels of Russian diesel each month for a two‑year period, with the oil being refined and then shipped to the United States via the Baltic Sea. Officials contend that the arrangement would provide a reliable source of low‑priced diesel at a time when crude oil markets are volatile, and that the revenue from the sales would be funneled into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. However, critics argue that the move effectively rewards a nation that has been sanctioned for its aggressive actions in Ukraine and could set a dangerous precedent for future engagements with sanctioned states.

Senators leading the opposition, including Republican Committee Chairman John Cornyn of Texas and Democratic Whip Dick Durbin of Illinois, stressed that the policy “runs counter to the very purpose of the sanctions regime” and could erode the credibility of U.S. diplomatic pressure on Moscow. “We cannot simultaneously punish Russia for its invasion and then hand it a lifeline through our own fuel markets,” Cornyn wrote. Durbin echoed the sentiment, adding that the plan could weaken alliances with European partners who have been bearing the brunt of Russian energy dependence and who have called for a unified front against Moscow’s aggression.

Energy analysts note that while the diesel deal might offer a short‑term price relief, the broader impact on the global oil market could be destabilizing. By creating a new demand channel for Russian refined products, the United States could inadvertently prop up Russian refiners, enabling them to reinvest earnings into further military spending. Moreover, the logistics of transporting diesel across the Baltic and Atlantic waters raise concerns about supply chain security, especially given the heightened risk of maritime interdiction in contested waters.

The administration, for its part, argues that the measure is a pragmatic response to domestic pressures. President Trump’s office has highlighted that fuel prices have risen to levels not seen in a decade, squeezing household budgets and threatening the economic recovery. In a recent briefing, Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm asserted that “leveraging all available sources, even those from sanctioned nations, is essential to protect American consumers.” The White House also pointed to the fact that the diesel would be purchased through a third‑party intermediary, thereby limiting direct financial flows to the Russian government.

The debate over the Russian diesel plan underscores a larger tension in U.S. policy: balancing immediate economic relief with long‑term strategic objectives. As Congress weighs the senators’ plea, the administration faces mounting pressure to present alternative solutions, such as boosting domestic refinery capacity, expanding strategic reserves, or negotiating with allied producers for temporary supply contracts. The outcome will likely shape not only fuel prices in the coming months but also the United States’ posture in the ongoing geopolitical contest with Russia.

Looking ahead, policymakers are expected to convene a bipartisan working group to explore viable alternatives that safeguard both the American economy and national security. If the administration heeds the senators’ call, the Russian diesel proposal could be abandoned in favor of measures that reinforce sanctions while still addressing domestic fuel concerns. The decision will serve as a litmus test for how the United States navigates the intersection of energy policy and foreign policy in an increasingly complex global landscape.
